Casey]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Tom Ridge]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsPA}} The '''1994 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election''' was held on November 8, 1994. The incumbent governor, [[Bob Casey Sr.|Bob Casey, Sr.]] (Democrat), was barred from seeking a third term by [[Pennsylvania Constitution|the state constitution]]. The [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]] nominated Congressman [[Tom Ridge]], while the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrats]] nominated [[Mark Singel]], Casey's [[Lieutenant Governor of Pennsylvania|lieutenant governor]]. Ridge went on to win the race with 45% of the vote. Singel finished with 39%, and [[Constitution Party (United States)|Constitution Party]] candidate Peg Luksik finished third, garnering 12% of the vote. ==Democratic primary== ===Candidates=== *[[Catherine Baker Knoll]], Pennsylvania Treasurer (from [[Allegheny County, Pennsylvania|Allegheny County]]) *[[Dwight Evans (politician)|Dwight Evans]], State Representative (from [[Philadelphia]]) *[[Bob O'Donnell]], State Representative and former Speaker of the House (from Philadelphia) *[[Mark Singel]], Lieutenant Governor (from [[Cambria County, Pennsylvania|Cambria County]]) *Phillip Valenti, [[LaRouche movement|LaRouche]] activist (from [[Chester County, Pennsylvania|Chester County]]) *Chuck Volpe, insurance executive (from Allegheny County) *[[Lynn Yeakel]], philanthropist and 1992 nominee for U.S. Senate (from [[Montgomery County, Pennsylvania|Montgomery County]]) ===Campaign=== Lt. Governor Singel was a well-known figure in the state and was a clear early frontrunner after serving six months as acting governor as [[Robert P. Casey|Bob Casey]] underwent cancer treatments. However, his 1992 defeat by [[Lynn Yeakel]] in the 1992 Democratic primary for senate left the party feeling that Singel was vulnerable in a statewide election. Treasurer [[Catherine Baker Knoll]], who was popular with older voters and siphoned the support of some labor groups from Singel, was viewed as his biggest threat, but state representative [[Dwight Evans (politician)|Dwight Evans]], who mobilized urban minority voters, finished a somewhat surprising second. Former state Speaker of the House [[Bob O'Donnell]] and Yeakel, who was criticized for campaigning poorly in the close 1992 senate race, both saw their campaigns fail to get traction. ===Results=== [[File:1994 Pennsylvania governor Democratic primary by county.svg|thumb|center|Democratic primary results {{collapsible list |title = {{legend|#7996E2|Singel}}|{{legend|#DFEEFF|20%–30%}}|{{legend|#BDD3FF|30%–40%}}|{{legend|#A5B0FF|40%–50%}}|{{legend|#7996E2|50%–60%}}|{{legend|#6674DE|60%–70%}} }} {{collapsible list |title = {{legend|#51C2C2|Evans}}|{{legend|#ACF2F2|30%–40%}}|{{legend|#51C2C2|50%–60%}} }} {{collapsible list |title = {{legend|#FFB380|Knoll}}|{{legend|#FEE5D5|30%–40%}}|{{legend|#FFCCAA|40%–50%}} }} {{collapsible list |title = {{legend|#F1C92A|Yeakel}}|{{legend|#FFF5CC|20%–30%}}|{{legend|#FFEEAA|30%–40%}} }} ]] {{Election box begin no change|title=Pennsylvania gubernatorial Democratic primary, 1994{{Cite web|url=https://www.ourcampaigns.com/RaceDetail.html?RaceID=40939|title = Our Campaigns - PA Governor - D Primary Race - May 10, 1994}}}} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change |party = Democratic Party (United States) |candidate = [[Mark Singel]] |votes = 346,344 |percentage = 31.19 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change |party = Democratic Party (United States) |candidate = [[Dwight E. Michael Fisher|Mike Fisher]], state senator and 1986 lieutenant governor nominee (from Allegheny County) *Jack Perry *[[Ernie Preate]], Pennsylvania Attorney General (from [[Lackawanna County, Pennsylvania|Lackawanna County]]) *[[Tom Ridge]], U.S. Representative from [[Erie, Pennsylvania|Erie]] (from [[Erie County, Pennsylvania|Erie County]]) ===Campaign=== Attorney General [[Ernie Preate]], who was known for both being a tough prosecutor and working to reform the mental health system, was seen as the initial frontrunner, but his attempt was marred by a corruption controversy. [[D. Michael Fisher|Mike Fisher]], a state senator and former candidate for lieutenant governor, sought to take advantage of Preate's missteps but was unable gain a majority of establishment support. [[Tom Ridge]], who Republicans had initially tried to court to run in the 1990 election, slowly built name recognition and gained political backing due to his relatively moderate track record. Governor (Democratic) **running mate: [[Tom Foley (Pennsylvania politician)|Tom Foley]], Pennsylvania Secretary of Labor and Industry *[[Tom Ridge]], U.S. Representative from [[Erie, Pennsylvania|Erie]] (Republican) **running mate: [[Mark Schweiker]], Bucks County Commissioner ===Campaign=== Prior to the election, Singel appeared to be a candidate who would be difficult to beat; he had gained wide name recognition and a positive job appraisal for his service as acting governor during [[Bob Casey Sr.|Bob Casey's]] battle with serious illness. In contrast, Ridge had been a relatively obscure Congressman who was mostly unknown outside of his [[Erie, Pennsylvania|Erie]] base. Ridge proved to be a successful fundraiser and undercut support from Democrats in the socially liberal but fiscally conservative suburbs of [[Philadelphia]] and [[Pittsburgh]].{{cite book|last=Kennedy|first=John J.|title=Pennsylvania Elections: Statewide Contests From 1950-2004|year=2006|publisher=University Press of America|isbn=9780761832799|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1J_9q-lIWRkC&q=1998+ridge+itkin&pg=PA112}} Abortion became a key issue in the campaign. Peg Luksik ran a strong third party campaign in opposition to the Republican nominations of the pro-choice Ridge and [[Barbara Hafer]] in their most recent two gubernatorial campaigns. Singel, who is also pro-choice, gained only lukewarm support from his former boss Casey, a vocal critic of abortion policy. The tide began to turn against Singel after the revelation that he had voted to parole an individual named [[Reginald McFadden]], who would later be charged for a series of murders in [[New York City]]. Ridge, whose campaign emphasized his "tough on crime" stance, took advantage of this situation, much in the manner that [[George H. W. Bush]] had used the [[Willie Horton]] incident against [[Michael Dukakis]].
